Sampled ranking metrics can reverse model comparisons relative to full-catalog evaluation, even in expectation ([Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). For RecHarness, preserve the pinned users, 99 negatives and evaluation seed; interpret results specifically as sampled-candidate HR@10. Fixed candidates support paired comparisons but do not establish full-catalog performance.

HR@10 with one held-out positive is binary per user. Compare checkpoints using each user’s hit difference, retaining model pairing; paired-binomial confidence intervals account for this dependence ([Fagerland et al.](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/sim.6148)). A practical diagnostic proposal is a paired bootstrap: resample users within each category, keep both models’ outcomes together, and recompute the equally weighted four-category mean difference. Report category changes alongside the macro change. With 200 users/category, one additional hit changes category HR by 0.005 and macro HR by 0.00125. Such intervals describe user-sampling uncertainty conditional on the fitted models and fixed candidates; they do not measure training-seed or candidate-resampling variability.

Repeated checkpoint selection and architecture search against the same validation users introduce adaptive selection bias; ordinary confidence intervals do not correct the winner’s optimism ([Dwork et al.](https://research.google/blog/the-reusable-holdout-preserving-validity-in-adaptive-data-analysis/)). Practical implications: predeclare checkpoint evaluation frequency and selection rules, record every inspected checkpoint/trial, and treat validation intervals as descriptive after selection. Keep training seed 42 and the evaluator unchanged; fixing the seed improves reproducibility but does not remove selection bias. Leave the final held-out assessment to the host after model selection.
